title: AI Gateway now supports Private Inference
summary:
Private Inference connects your own model endpoints to AI Gateway.

Enterprises running fine-tuned, self-hosted, or prerelease models used to need separate keys, client code, and logs for them. Those models can now run through the same authentication, SDKs and APIs, and observability as catalog models, so every model your team uses is managed in one place.

Use Private Inference to:

  • Switch between private and catalog models: Call private models through Chat Completions, Responses, or Messages. AI Gateway translates each request to your endpoint's format, so switching only changes the model ID.

  • Keep models scoped to your team: Only your Vercel team can view or call private models, and they aren't listed in the public catalog. Credentials are stored encrypted, and you can enable Zero Data Retention per provider.

  • Connect coding agents: Use private models in Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, and other coding agents connected to AI Gateway.

  • Monitor traffic together: View private model requests alongside catalog traffic in logs, trace drains, and custom reporting. Observability charts break down requests, tokens, and time to first token by private model.

  • Configure fallbacks: Optionally fall back to a catalog model if your private endpoint fails.

To get started, open the Private Inference page and add your endpoint as a private provider. Enter its base URL, select its API format, and add its credentials. Then add the models it serves.

title: Agents are users, so your software needs evals
summary:
Agents are now users of software, doing work on people's behalf. Whether you're building the agent or the software it uses (API, CLI, MCP server, SDK), evals give you a way to measure how well that work gets done.

Agents probably missed your launch video and billboard on Highway 101, but they still go through the same funnel a human does to find and use a product: Discovery, Selection, Access, and Success.

You can build evals for any stage of this funnel. Here, we’ll focus on the final stage, Success: whether the agent completes the user’s task correctly.

That's more difficult to check than it sounds. An agent can place a “successful” order for a hot latte when the user asked for an iced one. The request worked, so the logs in your Observability stack look fine. And because LLM outputs vary between runs, one good manual test can’t tell you whether a fix worked. You need to repeat the same tasks and grade the outcomes, before and after the change.

That’s what an eval is, a test you run many times and score. Here’s how we build one.

The agentic testing pyramid

If a test asks “did it work?”, an eval asks “how often does it work, and how well?”

We group agentic software tests by how many LLM calls they typically need: deterministic tests (0), one-turn evals (1), and E2E evals (2+ across a whole task). This has turned out to be a great proxy for the effort to build them, the time they take to run, and the cost of running them. Just like in the practical test pyramid, the cheap and fast tests should make up the bulk of your test suite.

To use the pyramid, start with the problem you want to catch and pick the lowest tier that can catch it. For Success, that's the top. A one-turn eval checks a single decision, like which command the agent runs first. But Success depends on the whole sequence of steps (e.g. search for cafes → filter on user criteria → place the latte order). Each one can look reasonable on its own, and the agent can still get the wrong outcome.

An E2E eval lets the agent work through the whole task in an environment, then checks whether the final result meets the user’s requirements. You’ve probably seen a few already; most popular coding benchmarks, like SWE-bench and Terminal-Bench, are E2E evals.

Example

Say you own SF Beans, an API for ordering coffee in San Francisco. One of the best ways to give agents access to your service is through a CLI, so you’re shipping sfbeans.

Here’s a typical request from one of your customers:

Get me a large iced latte with whole milk, ready for pickup by 9:00, under $8 including tip. I’m in the Mission.

Here’s what sfbeans knows at 8:30am:

  • Fog City Roasters: ice machine is down, so no iced drinks today (temperature)

  • 24th St Beans: latte is $7.50 on the menu, but $9.27 after tax and tip (budget)

  • Dolores Drip: latte is $5.50, but the earliest pickup is 9:20 (time)

  • Valencia Grind: $7.42 after tax and tip, ready at 8:50 (meets all three)

Here’s what you could test at each layer of the pyramid for sfbeans:

How to build an end-to-end eval

We’ll build the coffee eval with Harbor, an open-source framework from the creators of Terminal-Bench that runs agents in containers, checks results, and records their actions.

Here are the terms we’ll use:

  • Task: one problem for the agent to solve, with a starting environment and a way to check whether it succeeded

  • Variant: the agent setup you’re testing, like the model, prompt, tools, memory and skills

  • Trial: one attempt by one variant at one task

  • Run (a job in Harbor): every variant tried on every task, several times each

  • Trace (a trajectory in Harbor): everything recorded during a trial: messages, tool calls, logs, files and final output

Step 1: Set a goal

Building E2E evals for everything isn’t practical. With traditional software, you can aim for 100% test coverage. With agents, the surface you’d need to cover is everything an LLM might do with your product, and even figuring out where that ends is hard (see the jagged frontier).

Start with one outcome your users care about, narrow enough to evaluate with a handful of tasks. You’ll usually find that goal in one of three places:

  • Observability: which agents use your product, and where they fail

  • Customers: support tickets, feedback, and churn

  • Roadmap: the product hypotheses you most need to validate

For example, your goal might be to:

  • Increase the success rate on a specific task

  • Reduce the number of steps required to accomplish a goal

  • Check whether an agent skill helps, and get feedback to improve it

  • A/B test a prompt

  • Explore the frontier by checking whether a use case is achievable with current LLMs, and if they fail, why

Example

We looked in all three places for sfbeans:

  • Observability: Most agent traffic comes from Claude Code and Codex. We know because sfbeans adds a user-agent header when it detects a specific coding harness.

  • Customers: The top support ticket is “my agent ordered the wrong drink”: a hot latte instead of iced, a pickup after the user’s meeting, or a total over budget once tax and tip are added.

  • Roadmap: Nothing urgent, so the wrong-drink problem goes first, since it drives churn.

That gives us our goal:

Goal

Increase the success rate on ordering the exact drink the user asked for

Agents

Claude Code and Codex, since that’s where our traffic comes from.

In scope

Drink, pickup time, and budget (incl. tax and tip), using today’s sfbeans.

Out of scope

Cancellations, refunds, and accounts. We’ll eval those later.

Done when

Both agents get the order right in every trial, not just most of the time.

Step 2: Define metrics

Here are the metrics we use most for E2E agent evals:

Success

  • Success rate: the share of trials that pass

  • Pass@k: the chance that at least one of k trials passes (answers “can the agent do this at all?”)

  • Pass^k: the chance that all k trials pass (answers “can I rely on it every time?”)

Efficiency (measured on successful trials only)

  • Steps: the number of agent turns needed to complete the task

  • Time: how long the trial took

  • Cost: how much the trial cost, in dollars

What the numbers mean:

  • Success rate: 3 of 5 trials passed, so 60%.

  • Pass@5: Assuming independent trials with a 60% success rate, 1 − 0.4^5 ≈ 99%. Give the agent 5 tries and it almost certainly gets it right once.

  • Pass^5: 0.6^5 ≈ 8%. The chance the agent gets 5 orders in a row right.

So does Opus work? Its 99% pass@5 says yes. Its 8% pass^5 says a user who orders this every weekday gets at least one wrong coffee in 92% of weeks. Both numbers are right. They just answer different questions: pass@5 asks whether the agent can get the order right, and pass^5 asks whether it gets it right every time.

Which metric matters most depends on what a failure costs your user. Someone ordering their morning coffee doesn’t get a retry. If the agent orders a hot latte, or one that’s ready after their train leaves, they’ve paid for the wrong coffee and started their day annoyed. They need it right every morning, so sfbeans optimizes for pass^5.

Overall averages can hide a task that fails frequently, so always inspect results per task. And with only five trials, 100% means “no failures seen yet,” not “never fails.”

Step 3: Design the task set

In Step 1, we set a goal for the eval: increase how often agents order the exact drink the user asked for. But an agent can’t attempt a goal. It needs a task: one concrete request, drawn from what your users actually ask for.

Pick tasks hard enough that you learn something from running them. A good set covers the common case, the edge cases that trip agents up, and at least one request where the right move is not to act.

For each task, define these parts:

  • An instruction: the user’s request

  • An environment: where the agent works, with the same starting state for every trial

  • A verifier: a check of the final state, ideally scored per constraint

  • A known-good solution (optional): a reference run that demonstrates the expected behavior and passes the verifier

You can make every aspect of that environment as fake or as realistic as you need, depending on your goals. The OpenPipe team has a nice writeup on how they defined the environment for an email research agent.

Example

We wrote four tasks, each one a Harbor task folder in tasks/.

  • Common case: iced-latte-mission, the order from earlier

  • Edge case: usual-unavailable, where the user’s usual cafe is out of their drink

  • Edge case: team-order, with 6 drinks, $45 total, and one pickup spot

  • Don’t act: impossible-request, where nothing fits, so the right move is to tell the user

impossible-request has one extra check. Its verifier reads a command log the agent can’t write to, to confirm the agent searched before giving up. We learned we needed that the hard way (see Step 5).

Here’s iced-latte-mission:

The instruction gives the agent the user’s request and names the sfbeans CLI. In production, agents find the tool through a skill, docs, or an MCP server. Naming it here skips Discovery and Selection, keeping the eval focused on Success.

We also specify that it’s 8:30am. Only sfbeans uses our frozen clock; the sandbox’s system clock still shows the real time:

The environment is part real, part fake. The agent uses the real sfbeans CLI, but against seeded cafes and a frozen clock, so every trial starts on the same morning:

To keep the demo simple, cafes.json lives inside the agent’s environment. In a real eval, protect the seed data and verifier code, and make sure the agent can update order records only through the CLI. Agents can attempt to reward hack if it helps them pass, for example by editing the inventory or writing orders.json directly.

For this coffee order, the verifier checks the final order against the user’s requirements. Harbor runs test.sh after the agent finishes and reads the scores it writes to /logs/verifier/reward.json:

The actual check lives in check_orders.py. It scores each constraint separately, then sets reward to 1 only if all of them pass. Harbor uses reward as the trial’s main score:

The solution is a known-good answer. Run it before any real agent to prove the task works:

Finally, task.toml ties the task together. It sets the timeouts, runs the verifier in the agent’s sandbox (where orders.json lives), and saves the orders as an artifact so we can inspect them in Step 5:

Step 4: Run the eval

If you share the universal distaste for slow CI, you’ll hate waiting for evals. Every trial waits on an agent making LLM calls, step after step, and a run repeats that for every variant and task, several times each.

Harbor’s Vercel integration, which we built upstream, speeds that up a lot. It runs trials concurrently, each in its own Vercel Sandbox, and caches built task environments so they aren’t rebuilt for every trial. Routing model calls through AI Gateway gives you one key and one budget across model providers.

Example

Two agents, Claude Code and Codex, with two models each, make four variants.

Then install Harbor, connect a Vercel project, and run the job:

This run fits on the Hobby plan: 10 concurrent sandboxes is the Hobby limit, and each trial is well under its 45-minute session cap. On Pro, you can raise n_concurrent_trials as high as 10,000 (Sandbox limits).

To keep the example simple, we pass the OIDC token into each sandbox as an env var, where the agent can read it. Beyond a demo, use short-lived tokens, and use Harbor’s Vercel integration to set Sandbox firewall rules that lock each trial down to only the hosts it needs, like AI Gateway.

Internally, we go a step further and use credentials brokering to attach credentials to outgoing requests, keeping API keys outside the agent’s environment.

Step 5: Analyze traces

Now for the meaty part: trace-diving. Scores tell you how often your agents fail; traces tell you why. Read the failures, and some passes too, since a pass only means the verifier was satisfied.

Example

The run from Step 4 leaves 80 trial folders in jobs/sfbeans-baseline/. Each has the trial’s result, the agent’s trajectory, the verifier’s scores, and, because task.toml saves it as an artifact, the order the agent placed:

That’s our baseline. On pass^5, the metric we chose in Step 2, even the best variant is far from reliable. But the score doesn’t tell us what to fix. For that, we have to open the failed trials.

Take trial 2 from Step 2. Claude Code + Opus 5.5 ordered at 24th St Beans for $9.27. The verifier tells us which constraint it broke:

Right drink, on time, over budget, and the saved orders.json confirms the $9.27 total. Now we read agent/trajectory.json. The agent searches for lattes in the Mission, sees $7.50 on the menu, and goes straight to order. No quote. It treated the menu price as the final price.

Trial 1, from the same variant, quotes three cafes, rules out 24th St Beans, and orders at Valencia Grind for $7.42. So the CLI can get the order right, but the agent doesn’t reliably check the total before spending the user’s money.

We then look for that pattern across other failed trials, and if it keeps showing up, we have something specific to fix: make the total harder to miss, or add a --max-total flag so order refuses anything over budget. That’s a much more useful conclusion than “Opus scored 85%.”

When we first ran this demo, the traces also exposed problems with what the eval was measuring:

  • Our first run scored 0% on every variant. The agents didn’t know sfbeans existed, so they never tried it (obviously). That’s the funnel’s Discovery stage failing in our own eval. Naming the tool in the instruction fixed it, and it’s a good reminder that being discoverable is part of your product. In the wild, that’s the job of your skill, docs, MCP server and AEO.

  • Codex kept looking for sfbeans as a connected tool and never tried running it in the shell. That’s an Access problem, not a Success one.

  • Codex passed impossible-request almost every time, but when we read the traces, 9 out of 10 passes were the agent giving up without looking. The verifier only checked that no order was placed, so we tightened it to also check that the agent searched first. Without reading the traces, we’d have counted those as wins.

Automated trace analysis

For larger runs, inspecting every trial by hand gets slow, so we automate it.

Up to 40 reader agents running fast models like deepseek/deepseek-v4.1-flash read trial transcripts in parallel and summarize their findings. A smarter coordinator agent reviews those summaries, sends readers back for more context when needed, and writes the final report. An analysis.md file tells the coordinator what to look for, so we can reuse the workflow across runs.

Model calls go through AI Gateway. Trial artifacts stay in Vercel Drives during analysis, and traces go to Vercel Blob for long-term storage.

Iterate to greatness

Your first eval run gives you a baseline. Now act on it.

Pick the fix the traces point to, like the --max-total flag, rerun the same job, and compare against the baseline. Check whether it reduces the targeted failures without introducing new ones, then use those results to decide whether the change is ready to ship.

Once you’ve built an eval, it keeps paying off for a lot of different things. Rerun it on every release to catch regressions; test prompt, skill, and model changes before shipping; learn how agents use your product; or build auto-optimization loops on top of it.

Expect to add harder tasks over time. As models and your product improve, evals saturate, meaning agents start passing every task. A saturated eval still catches regressions, but it can’t tell you what to improve next.

Evals are the infrastructure you use to make your product better, again and again. Vercel has the pieces you need to build them in one place: AI Gateway for model calls across providers, Sandbox to run trials at scale, and Drives and Blob to keep every trace.

Which metric matters most depends on what a failure costs your user. Someone ordering their morning coffee doesn’t get a retry. If the agent orders a hot latte, or one that’s ready after their train leaves, they’ve paid for the wrong coffee and started their day annoyed. They need it right every morning, so sfbeans optimizes for pass^5.

Step 3: Design the task set

In Step 1, we set a goal for the eval: increase how often agents order the exact drink the user asked for. But an agent can’t attempt a goal. It needs a task: one concrete request, drawn from what your users actually ask for.

Pick tasks hard enough that you learn something from running them. A good set covers the common case, the edge cases that trip agents up, and at least one request where the right move is not to act.

For each task, define these parts:

  • An instruction: the user’s request

  • An environment: where the agent works, with the same starting state for every trial

  • A verifier: a check of the final state, ideally scored per constraint

  • A known-good solution (optional): a reference run that demonstrates the expected behavior and passes the verifier

You can make every aspect of that environment as fake or as realistic as you need, depending on your goals. The OpenPipe team has a nice writeup on how they defined the environment for an email research agent.

Example

We wrote four tasks, each one a Harbor task folder in tasks/.

  • Common case: iced-latte-mission, the order from earlier

  • Edge case: usual-unavailable, where the user’s usual cafe is out of their drink

  • Edge case: team-order, with 6 drinks, $45 total, and one pickup spot

  • Don’t act: impossible-request, where nothing fits, so the right move is to tell the user

impossible-request has one extra check. Its verifier reads a command log the agent can’t write to, to confirm the agent searched before giving up. We learned we needed that the hard way (see Step 5).

Here’s iced-latte-mission:

The instruction gives the agent the user’s request and names the sfbeans CLI. In production, agents find the tool through a skill, docs, or an MCP server. Naming it here skips Discovery and Selection, keeping the eval focused on Success.

We also specify that it’s 8:30am. Only sfbeans uses our frozen clock; the sandbox’s system clock still shows the real time:

The environment is part real, part fake. The agent uses the real sfbeans CLI, but against seeded cafes and a frozen clock, so every trial starts on the same morning:

To keep the demo simple, cafes.json lives inside the agent’s environment. In a real eval, protect the seed data and verifier code, and make sure the agent can update order records only through the CLI. Agents can attempt to reward hack if it helps them pass, for example by editing the inventory or writing orders.json directly.

For this coffee order, the verifier checks the final order against the user’s requirements. Harbor runs test.sh after the agent finishes and reads the scores it writes to /logs/verifier/reward.json:

The actual check lives in check_orders.py. It scores each constraint separately, then sets reward to 1 only if all of them pass. Harbor uses reward as the trial’s main score:

The solution is a known-good answer. Run it before any real agent to prove the task works:

Finally, task.toml ties the task together. It sets the timeouts, runs the verifier in the agent’s sandbox (where orders.json lives), and saves the orders as an artifact so we can inspect them in Step 5:

Step 4: Run the eval

If you share the universal distaste for slow CI, you’ll hate waiting for evals. Every trial waits on an agent making LLM calls, step after step, and a run repeats that for every variant and task, several times each.

Harbor’s Vercel integration, which we built upstream, speeds that up a lot. It runs trials concurrently, each in its own Vercel Sandbox, and caches built task environments so they aren’t rebuilt for every trial. Routing model calls through AI Gateway gives you one key and one budget across model providers.

Example

Two agents, Claude Code and Codex, with two models each, make four variants.

Then install Harbor, connect a Vercel project, and run the job:

This run fits on the Hobby plan: 10 concurrent sandboxes is the Hobby limit, and each trial is well under its 45-minute session cap. On Pro, you can raise n_concurrent_trials as high as 10,000 (Sandbox limits).

To keep the example simple, we pass the OIDC token into each sandbox as an env var, where the agent can read it. Beyond a demo, use short-lived tokens, and use Harbor’s Vercel integration to set Sandbox firewall rules that lock each trial down to only the hosts it needs, like AI Gateway.

Internally, we go a step further and use credentials brokering to attach credentials to outgoing requests, keeping API keys outside the agent’s environment.

Step 5: Analyze traces

Now for the meaty part: trace-diving. Scores tell you how often your agents fail; traces tell you why. Read the failures, and some passes too, since a pass only means the verifier was satisfied.

Example

The run from Step 4 leaves 80 trial folders in jobs/sfbeans-baseline/. Each has the trial’s result, the agent’s trajectory, the verifier’s scores, and, because task.toml saves it as an artifact, the order the agent placed:

That’s our baseline. On pass^5, the metric we chose in Step 2, even the best variant is far from reliable. But the score doesn’t tell us what to fix. For that, we have to open the failed trials.

Take trial 2 from Step 2. Claude Code + Opus 5.5 ordered at 24th St Beans for $9.27. The verifier tells us which constraint it broke:

Right drink, on time, over budget, and the saved orders.json confirms the $9.27 total. Now we read agent/trajectory.json. The agent searches for lattes in the Mission, sees $7.50 on the menu, and goes straight to order. No quote. It treated the menu price as the final price.

Trial 1, from the same variant, quotes three cafes, rules out 24th St Beans, and orders at Valencia Grind for $7.42. So the CLI can get the order right, but the agent doesn’t reliably check the total before spending the user’s money.

We then look for that pattern across other failed trials, and if it keeps showing up, we have something specific to fix: make the total harder to miss, or add a --max-total flag so order refuses anything over budget. That’s a much more useful conclusion than “Opus scored 85%.”

When we first ran this demo, the traces also exposed problems with what the eval was measuring:

  • Our first run scored 0% on every variant. The agents didn’t know sfbeans existed, so they never tried it (obviously). That’s the funnel’s Discovery stage failing in our own eval. Naming the tool in the instruction fixed it, and it’s a good reminder that being discoverable is part of your product. In the wild, that’s the job of your skill, docs, MCP server and AEO.

  • Codex kept looking for sfbeans as a connected tool and never tried running it in the shell. That’s an Access problem, not a Success one.

  • Codex passed impossible-request almost every time, but when we read the traces, 9 out of 10 passes were the agent giving up without looking. The verifier only checked that no order was placed, so we tightened it to also check that the agent searched first. Without reading the traces, we’d have counted those as wins.

Automated trace analysis

For larger runs, inspecting every trial by hand gets slow, so we automate it.

Up to 40 reader agents running fast models like deepseek/deepseek-v4.1-flash read trial transcripts in parallel and summarize their findings. A smarter coordinator agent reviews those summaries, sends readers back for more context when needed, and writes the final report. An analysis.md file tells the coordinator what to look for, so we can reuse the workflow across runs.

Model calls go through AI Gateway. Trial artifacts stay in Vercel Drives during analysis, and traces go to Vercel Blob for long-term storage.

Iterate to greatness

Your first eval run gives you a baseline. Now act on it.

Pick the fix the traces point to, like the --max-total flag, rerun the same job, and compare against the baseline. Check whether it reduces the targeted failures without introducing new ones, then use those results to decide whether the change is ready to ship.

Once you’ve built an eval, it keeps paying off for a lot of different things. Rerun it on every release to catch regressions; test prompt, skill, and model changes before shipping; learn how agents use your product; or build auto-optimization loops on top of it.

Expect to add harder tasks over time. As models and your product improve, evals saturate, meaning agents start passing every task. A saturated eval still catches regressions, but it can’t tell you what to improve next.

Evals are the infrastructure you use to make your product better, again and again. Vercel has the pieces you need to build them in one place: AI Gateway for model calls across providers, Sandbox to run trials at scale, and Drives and Blob to keep every trace.

title: Workflow SDK 5: built for production
summary:
When we first launched Workflow SDK, the goal was simple: write regular async JavaScript, and let the SDK keep it running through crashes, deployments, and long waits.

Last year, we shipped just that, with the world-class developer experience Vercel is known for. Then we watched what our customers built with it.

More than 4 billion steps and 700 million runs later, two clear patterns have emerged.

  • The first is automation: Traditional workflows that move data, process orders, coordinate background jobs, manage subscriptions, and run ETL and data pipelines.

  • The second is agents and harnesses: Agents are expensive and long running, so they naturally require durability too.

As those workloads matured, Workflow matured with them. Our priorities have always been security, reliability, and performance.

Here’s how Workflow SDK 5 delivers on all three.

More secure workflows

The Workflow event log stores step arguments and return values so a run can recover after a crash or deployment. That data can include sensitive customer information, model context, credentials, and tool-call results. Persisting it requires strong protection.

Workflow SDK encrypts every payload end to end, before it leaves your code. Workflow and step inputs and outputs, hook payloads, and stream data are encrypted with AES-256-GCM, using a unique key for each run. With encryption enabled, any Workflow SDK backend, including Vercel, only sees and stores ciphertext. Plaintext is decrypted in your deployment or in authorized observability tools.

Encryption with zero configuration on Vercel

On Vercel, encryption needs no setup and no code changes. Each run’s key is derived from a key scoped to the deployment that created it, so a run can only decrypt its own data. Your workflow code doesn’t change:

title: Vercel Sandbox now supports managed npm credentials
summary:

Tokens stay outside the sandbox. The firewall adds authentication to install requests sent to your configured registries, so a coding agent can install dependencies without seeing the tokens.

Update your Sandbox SDK or CLI to the latest version.

Read the npm credentials documentation to get started.

title: Speed Insights and Web Analytics now support custom environments
summary:
Speed Insights and Web Analytics now fully support custom environments.

Previously, data captured on deployments to a custom environment was attributed to the Preview environment. That data is now attributed to the custom environment it came from, so you can track performance and traffic for staging, QA, or canary environments separately from Production and Preview.

You can view this data in several places:

  • Dashboard: use the Environment dropdown in Speed Insights and Web Analytics to pick a custom environment

  • CLI: query it with the vc metrics command

  • Query builder: filter and break down by environment

  • Aggregation API: query it programmatically (Web Analytics only)

This change only affects how data is attributed. No new data points are collected, and no configuration changes are needed.

Custom environments are available on Pro and Enterprise plans. Learn more in the environments documentation.

title: Vercel Sandbox snapshot creation is now up to 10x faster
summary:
Vercel Sandbox now creates snapshots up to 10x faster. Median time to snapshot is under 0.4 seconds, down from 4.4 seconds. Snapshot restore speed has also improved by 50% from 500ms to 250ms at p50.

Snapshots are now able to write and restore by re-using frames within the Vercel Hive Snapshot (VHS) format. VHS now indexes data in a more efficient way which means that more read and write operations can be done in parallel. Snapshots can now restore more of your Sandbox base image in parallel with user data, leading to overall faster operations.

Persistent sandboxes, the default, snapshot automatically when a session stops and resume from the latest snapshot. This applies to all new snapshots, with nothing to configure. Existing snapshots keep the previous format.

Learn more in the snapshots documentation.

title: Decision models take 26% of requests; Anthropic now wins new teams 2:1
summary:
AI Gateway Production Index — November 2026

Every month, AI Gateway routes more than 100 trillion tokens between production applications and AI labs. That traffic gives us a view of what AI usage looks like in today’s enterprise and startup landscape across language, decision, voice, image, and video models. We publish it here monthly. See the Production Index reports from August, September, and October.

November 2026 Summary

  • In six weeks, decision models grew to one in four gateway requests, while accounting for half a cent of every dollar spent. Close to a third of all paid teams used one in October. Among teams processing over 10 billion tokens a month, seven in ten used a decision model.

  • About 11% of paid teams used a voice model in October, up from 4% in July.

  • OpenAI and Anthropic now reach about the same share of paid teams, and new teams in October picked Anthropic nearly two to one. OpenAI’s share of gateway spend, meanwhile, is up by two-thirds since December.

  • More than half of language-model requests went to models less than two months old, up from less than three in ten. Within one month of a typical model’s peak usage, three in four of the teams using it have moved on.

Decision models account for 26% of all requests

Production AI is splitting into two jobs: generation and judgment. Until recently, when software needed to make a quick call, a team could use either a fixed rule that was cheap but rigid, or a language model that was smart but slow and expensive.

Decision models are now a third option. They classify, score, or pick between choices instead of generating text, and cost about a seventieth as much per request as a language model.

They arrived on AI Gateway in mid-September, and there are now 15 decision models available from eight different vendors. In October, nearly a third of paid teams on AI Gateway used a decision model. About 11% of paid teams used a decision model without sending a single request to a text-generating model.

Decision models cost far less per token and give very short answers, so even though they received about one in four gateway requests in October, they accounted for just 0.53% of total spend.

Almost all of that request volume went to Jev from TypeSafe AI, which alone received nearly four times Anthropic’s total requests. For every $1 teams spent on Jev, they spent $64 on Anthropic models.

Decision models are most common among the teams that run the most AI. Just over one in five teams running fewer than 10 million tokens used a decision model in October. At 100 million to 1 billion tokens, nearly half used one. Above 10 billion, seven in ten did.

This is partly because big teams use more of everything. The top 1% of teams by spend use a median of 29 different models, and the bottom tenth use only one. It’s also volume. The more requests a team sends, the more it has to gain from a model that makes simple decisions faster and far more cost-effectively.

Voice adoption is up 2.6x since July

About one in nine paid teams used a voice model in October, up from one in 24 in July, an increase of 161%.

New teams are using voice, and existing teams are adding it. Among teams that paid in both July and October, the share using voice went from 5% to 14%.

Teams that use voice are also using more of it. The share of teams sending at least 100 voice requests a month grew fivefold, and six in ten of September’s voice teams returned in October, up from fewer than half in July.

A spoken conversation with an AI app takes three steps:

  • A voice model turns the user’s speech into text

  • A language model writes the reply

  • Another voice model reads the reply back to the user

Most voice teams use just one or two of these pieces. Use of speech-to-text models has nearly tripled since July, and text-to-speech has more than tripled.

Some models do all three steps on their own. In July, about a quarter of voice teams used one of these all-in-one models, and one in six assembled the pieces themselves. By October, those numbers had swapped.

For most teams, voice is a new way for users to talk to an app or agent they already have. Teams’ preferred language models stay in the middle, and they can add voice at one end or both.

Anthropic wins new teams two to one, and OpenAI’s share of spend is up two-thirds

Last December, 70 of every 100 paid teams on AI Gateway used an OpenAI model and 48 used an Anthropic model. By October, the two labs were nearly level, with OpenAI at 55 and Anthropic at 54.

Both labs now reach more of the teams that have been on the gateway since December, but Anthropic’s reach grew more. The share of these teams using Anthropic rose from about half to two-thirds, while OpenAI’s rose from about three in four to four in five.

Most of Anthropic’s gain came from new teams. In October, it was the first-choice lab for nearly twice as many of them as OpenAI.

But among the biggest teams, both labs already have nearly everyone. More than nine in ten of the top 1% by spend use both Anthropic and OpenAI. With these teams, the labs now compete for how much of the work each one gets.

On that measure, Anthropic still leads, but OpenAI has gained ground. OpenAI now takes nearly 15 cents of every dollar spent on the gateway, up from about 9 in December, while Anthropic’s halved to about 32 cents over the same period.

Most AI traffic now runs on models less than two months old

Teams are moving to new models almost as fast as labs release them. More than half of October’s language-model requests went to models less than 60 days old. Before September, that share had never passed three in ten.

Within each model family, a new version arrives every 61 days at the median, and a typical model peaks within a month of launch. Four weeks later, three in four of the teams using it at its peak aren’t using it anymore, whether or not a successor has shipped in the family. Most of those teams are still on AI Gateway, using other models.

Teams switch models frequently, usually to something newer, and often to another lab. In October, about half of teams running at least 10 million tokens a month changed their most-used model. Four in five of those moved to a more recent release, and six in ten moved to a different lab.

Older models stay in use, often alongside a newer primary model. Seven in ten teams running at least 10 million tokens a month still used a model at least ten months old in October, but for the typical team it ran less than 3% of its tokens.

AI models now have a half-life of about six weeks. That means that, to the teams using them, labs are only as good as their latest model and have to re-earn their business with every new one.

Also in October’s data

  • Opus 5.5 was the top model by spend in its first full month. It took about one in seven dollars across all teams. Four of the six most widely used models on AI Gateway are Anthropic’s: Sonnet 5.5 (reaching 26% of paid teams), Haiku 5.5 (22%), Haiku 4.5 (20%), and Opus 5.5 (18%). Jev (28%) and GPT-6 Luna (19%) are the other two.

  • Image and video both had their biggest month yet on AI Gateway. More teams than ever are putting spend on them, and the largest teams are adopting them the fastest. About a third of the top 1% of teams by spend now use an image model, up from a quarter in July. One in six use a video model, up from one in ten.

  • OpenAI’s newest image model, GPT-Image-2.5 Sunburst, took the lead in image spend in its first full month, followed by its Flare and GPT-Image-2 models. ByteDance’s Seedance 2.5 led video spend for a third month running, ahead of Google’s Veo 3.1 and Kuaishou’s Kling 3.0.

About this data

This report uses anonymized, aggregate traffic routed through Vercel AI Gateway through October 2026.

A few notes on measurement:

  • Spend is estimated at published list prices; actual bills may differ.

  • Paid teams are teams with at least one paid request in the month. Team size is measured by a team’s total tokens that month.

  • Decision models are the models classified as decision models in the AI Gateway model list.

  • Each model version is counted separately. A model’s age is measured from that version’s first day on AI Gateway, and gateway history begins October 20, 2025.

  • Switching rates compare paid teams with at least 10 million tokens in both September and October. A team’s most-used model is measured by tokens.

  • Voice figures begin June 22, 2026. Teams that “assembled the pieces” used speech-to-text, a language model, and text-to-speech on the same day.

  • A new team’s first-choice lab is the lab it sent the most language-model requests to in its first month.

  • All figures use the most recent data and protocol available; prior months may be revised as methodology is updated.

Read more about our methodology, and explore or download the public data.

title: Workflow SDK now writes over WebSockets on Vercel
summary:
The Workflow SDK now sends event writes and stream writes to Vercel Workflows over a WebSocket by default, replacing one HTTP request per write, or per write group for streams. No code change is needed beyond upgrading to workflow@5.2.0 or later.

Once you deploy the upgrade, new runs use it. In-flight runs finish on the deployment they started on.

Existing streaming code works as is. A step that writes a burst of chunks, like AI tokens, sends them over the WebSocket once it opens:

Streams keep pace with AI output

In a benchmark replaying an AI agent's token stream, v5.2.0, which writes streams over a WebSocket by default, delivered the full response 4.2× faster than v4.8.12, with no chunk delayed over a second.

Fewer HTTP requests for event writes

Every step start and completion is an event write, now sent over the WebSocket, so workflows with many steps make fewer HTTP requests. The added efficiency also improves performance and reduces costs. The queue handler opens the connection for every delivery.

Get started

Read the Vercel World documentation to get started. If you're on 4.x, start with the upgrade guide, since v5 is a major release.

title: Vercel Container Registry now supports 2 GB compressed image layers
summary:
Vercel Container Registry now supports compressed image layers of up to 2 GB each, up from 500 MB, the total image size limit stays 15 GB.

The registry works with standard workflows like docker push, docker pull, and docker tag, and pushing an image creates the repository on the fly.

Repositories can be made public for read-only pull access by any Vercel team, or shared with specific teams up to 100 from the dashboard or with vercel vcr permissions. The Vercel Managed Images that Vercel Sandbox runs on are served from ordinary public repositories, built with the same public-repository feature any team can use for its own images.

Manage repositories, images, and tags with the vercel vcr CLI commands in Vercel CLI v58.3.0 or later, and log CI workflows in from GitHub Actions with the vercel/vcr-action/login action using GitHub OIDC, which removes the need for long-lived registry credentials. If background optimization of a pushed image fails, the image shows an error status in the dashboard, and pushing the same image again retries the conversion.

See the documentation for the full setup.

title: Claude Fable 5.2 now available on AI Gateway
summary:
Claude Fable 5.2 from Anthropic is now available on AI Gateway.

Fable 5.2 is built for open-ended technical work and improves on earlier Fable models in coding, reasoning, and vision. It can run long, ambiguous tasks unattended, and works as an orchestrator that hands simpler tasks to smaller models, or as an advisor that other Claude models consult on harder problems. It also communicates more clearly and generates output faster than earlier Fable models. Effort runs from low to max, with high as the API default.

Fable 5.2 has cybersecurity and biology safety classifiers enabled. Access to Claude Fable 5.2 requires data retention. Anthropic does not support Zero Data Retention for the model. Prompts and completions are retained for 30 days and are not used to train Claude. If your team has ZDR turned on, AI Gateway returns an error instead of sending the request to Fable 5.2.

To keep requests served when a classifier is triggered, use model fallbacks. Add a models array to providerOptions.gateway, and AI Gateway tries each model in order when the cybersecurity classifier declines a request.

Call it through the AI SDK, the Chat Completions, Responses, and Anthropic Messages APIs, or a coding agent connected to AI Gateway. Use anthropic/claude-fable-5.2 as the model name:

This request falls back to Opus 5.5, then Sonnet 5.5, if the cybersecurity classifier declines it. The models option works the same way on every AI Gateway API format.

Try Claude Fable 5.2 in the model playground.

This request falls back to Opus 5.5, then Sonnet 5.5, if the cybersecurity classifier declines it. The models option works the same way on every AI Gateway API format.
